2.text: Relatives by affinity are called collectively mataˊlit (pl.) or mataˊlɪ-raˊmkɪn

4.text: Men married to two sisters call each other takaˊlhɪn. Takaˊlhɪn more

5.text: properly signifies “brace-companion;” for instance, one of the two reindeer

6.text: harnessed to the sledge. Pɪtkaˊ-takaˊlhɪn signifies “twin-brother” (literally,

7.text: “double-companion”). The degree of affinity thus indicated is considered to

8.text: be very strong. In olden times it was considered even stronger than brother-

9.text: hood. Takaˊlhɪn kɪrñaˊ-yêˊčamêt-tɵmg̣êˊpu paˊroč signifies “man of the wife’s

10.text: sister (is) of the old-male-brother beyond.” An old proverb says, “Man of

11.text: the wife’s sister is on the same lake shore a fall-companion” (takaˊlhɪn ᴇnnaˊn-

12.text: hɪˊthɪlɪñkɪ rɪlteˊl-tɵˊmg̣ɪn). This means that both are to fight and fall together.

13.text: The Chukchee say that if one takaˊlhɪn sees the blood of the other drawn

14.text: by an enemy, he will rush forward again and again until his own body lies

18.text: The family is designated as raˊyɪrɪn (“houseful,” or simply “those in the

19.text: house”), yaraˊ-tɵˊmg̣ɪt (“house-mates”); but both these terms relate, properly

20.text: speaking, to the house and those living in it. The house with those living

21.text: in it forms the real basis of the Chukchee family. Members of the family

22.text: who have left the house (or, among the Reindeer Chukchee, the camp) lose

23.text: their connection with the household and also with the family.
